title: Disable or Modify Tools
summary: Disable or Modify Tools is the broad degradation of defensive controls and of the sensors that feed detection. Adversaries stop security services, kill their processes, edit configuration files and registry keys, block product updates, and tamper with logging pipelines such as Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), audit policy, and central log forwarding. The objective is not only evasion of a single alert but a durable loss of visibility that lets later actions, commonly ransomware deployment, proceed unnoticed. Artefacts concentrate in the configuration and service-management plane rather than in file execution: service state changes, registry modifications to service and autologger keys, new audit policy values, and abrupt gaps in a previously continuous log stream. Legitimate administrative change produces the same events, so defenders separate the two by tying each change to a change record or ticket, to an expected operator identity, and to a change window, then treating unlinked tampering as the counterpart to the same request.

beginner.definition: This technique means an attacker weakens or turns off the tools that watch a system. Those tools include antivirus programs, endpoint sensors, and the logs that record what happens. The attacker may stop a service, change a setting, or block an update. The aim is to work without being seen or recorded.
beginner.whyItMatters: If the cameras are off, nobody sees what happens next. Attackers often do this just before stealing data or starting ransomware. Strange activity then leaves no evidence, so the response team arrives late. Because normal administrators also stop services, you must be able to tell planned work apart from tampering.
howItWorks: The attacker gains administrator rights on a host or high permissions in a cloud account.
They identify the security tools and logging agents running on the system.
They stop the related services, or kill the processes that belong to them.
They change configuration files, registry keys, or audit settings so the tools stay off.
They may block updates, or interrupt the flow of logs to the central collector.
With the sensors quiet, they continue with theft, movement, or encryption.
beginner.example: Think of a shop where the security guard is sent home early by someone with the right paperwork. The cameras still hang on the wall, and the alarm box still blinks. Nothing looks broken from the street. The theft happens quietly overnight, and the morning staff must rebuild the story from memory.
takeaways: Watch service, driver, and audit configuration changes, not just running processes.
Compare tool configuration against a known good baseline on a schedule.
Forward and protect logs off the host so tampering cannot erase them.

objectives: Explain what it means to degrade a defensive tool and why attackers do it.
List the main tampering methods, such as stopping services and blocking updates.
Describe why logging pipelines and sensors are targets in their own right.
Identify the configuration-plane artefacts that reveal tampering after the fact.
Explain how to distinguish approved administrative change from malicious change.
